name: Egyptian cosmetic palettes

card.summary: Carved stone slabs from ancient Egypt on which mineral pigments such as malachite were ground into the eye paint and body color people wore to enhance their appearance.
card.aka: Predynastic palettes; slate palettes; Narmer Palette (ceremonial type)

quick.overview:
Egyptian cosmetic palettes are flat stone surfaces, often shaped like fish, turtles, birds or rhombs, used from the Predynastic period to grind mineral pigments into cosmetics. Green malachite and dark galena were turned into the eye paint worn by people of many social classes.

The appearance payoff was defined, darkened or green-tinted eyes and colored skin. Archaeology shows the palettes in graves, usually near the hands or face, and later large carved ceremonial versions, such as the Narmer Palette, that no longer show grinding wear.
quick.how: A small pebble, often jasper, was used to crush the mineral on the stone, and the powder was mixed with resin, oil or fat to make a paste for the eyelids or body. Thick rectangular grinding palettes remained in use into the Old and Middle Kingdoms.
quick.risks: Ancient eye paint was based on minerals such as lead sulfide (galena); modern analyses of kohl have linked some products to higher blood lead levels. Egyptian palettes themselves are archaeological objects, not a product in current use.

lead: Egyptian cosmetic palettes are stone surfaces used to grind pigments for cosmetics. They are especially characteristic of Predynastic Egypt, where purpose-shaped palettes appear from the Badarian period and become common in burials.[1]

The pigments ground on them gave people the eye definition and body color that were central to Egyptian grooming. Malachite is the pigment most often found on burial palettes; galena, hematite and red ochre also occur.[1] Ancient Egyptians used galena for black and malachite for green eye paint, and kohl use is dated to about 3100 BCE, worn across social classes.[2]
Over time, large relief-carved palettes appeared in Naqada III (about 3200-3100 BCE) and are linked to early royal imagery; they keep the circular grinding area but show no wear.[1]

chain: Mineral such as malachite or galena ground on stone palette
Powder mixed with fat, oil or resin into paint
Defined, colored eyes and decorated skin
angle.text: The palette was the tool that turned raw minerals into usable makeup. Egyptians applied the resulting paint to the eyelids, typically black on the upper and green on the lower, to define and color the eyes.

infobox: Badarian to Old/Middle Kingdom; flat decorative types peak Naqada I-III[1]
Mostly grey-green stone from Wadi Hammamat; also limestone, quartz[1]
Narmer Palette, Cairo (JE32169), about 63 cm high[1]

paras: Stone surfaces for grinding color appear at Palaeolithic and Neolithic sites; purpose-shaped palettes appear in the Badarian period. Naqada I favored rhomboid forms, and Naqada II brought fish, turtle, bird and shield shapes.[1] From the Badarian onward, Upper Egyptian palettes were almost exclusively grey-green stone from Wadi Hammamat, with limestone and quartz examples also known.[1]

Pigments were mixed with resins, oils or fats and ground with small pebbles, often jasper.[1] Flat grey-stone palettes had disappeared by the middle of the First Dynasty, while thick rectangular grinding palettes continued into the Old and Middle Kingdoms.[1]

Palettes appear in burials, usually near the hands or face; in the cemeteries examined by Stevenson about 15 percent of graves had one, more often female burials.[1] Malachite preserved on bodies at Adaima suggests green pigment was applied to the skin.[1]

Eye paint was worn by people of all classes; upper lids were typically painted black and lower lids green. Egyptians also believed it protected the eyes from sunlight and disease, and the Ebers Papyrus (c. 1550 BCE) describes its protective role.[2] Under Hatshepsut charred frankincense was also ground into kohl.[2]

Large relief-carved ceremonial palettes of Naqada III are linked to the emergence of royal imagery. The Narmer Palette, found in the Main Deposit at Hierakonpolis, shows the king in the White Crown on one face and Red Crown on the other and carries some of the earliest known hieroglyphs.[1] Many ceremonial palettes keep a circular grinding area derived from small palettes but show no sign of grinding.[1]

sections.h: Health aspects of ancient eye paint
paras: A 2010 French study reported that certain lead compounds in the paint could stimulate nitric oxide production, which the authors suggested might support immune response, and one test found antimicrobial activity.[2] Studies from the early 1990s found high lead levels in some commercial kohl and linked kohl use to higher blood lead levels.[2]
No studies found of the palettes themselves. Laboratory analyses of kohl and ancient eye-paint composition exist, as described above.[2]

timeline.event: Large ceremonial palettes appear in Naqada III.[1]
Kohl use is dated to this period.[2]
Ebers Papyrus describes the protective role of eye paint.[2]
